title: Messy Bookshelf
statement:
A bookshelf holds **n** books with numbers a[1], ..., a[n] written on their spines. The shelf is "messy" in proportion to its number of **inversions**: pairs of positions (i, j) where i is to the left of j but a[i] is greater than a[j] (a bigger number stands to the left of a smaller one). Equal numbers do not form an inversion.

Count the inversions.
input:
The first line contains an integer **n**.

The second line contains n integers a[1], ..., a[n].
output: Print one integer: the number of inversions.
hints: Checking all pairs takes O(n^2) time: too slow for 2·10^5.
Use merge sort. When an element of the right half is placed before the remaining elements of the left half, each of those remaining elements forms an inversion with it.
The answer can be about 2·10^10: use 64-bit integers. Take elements from the left half when they are equal, so equal pairs are not counted.
editorial:
Modify merge sort. Sort the left and right halves recursively and count their inversions; then merge them. During the merge, if the next element of the right half is strictly smaller than the next element of the left half, it is smaller than **all** remaining left elements, so add the number of remaining left elements to the answer. On ties, take the left element first so equal values are not counted. The total is the sum over all merges.

A Fenwick tree over compressed values is another O(n log n) solution.

Complexity: O(n log n).
